Gallai lemma: a three-coloring without rainbow triangles has a disconnected color
In every edge-coloring of a complete graph with three colors, if no triangle has three pairwise distinct edge colors, then at least one of the three color classes is disconnected as a spanning graph.
Three connected colors force a rainbow triangle
The contrapositive form is useful in applications: a three-coloring of a complete graph with all three color classes connected must contain a rainbow triangle.
Reference proof

Gyarfás and Simonyi state this as Lemma A and give a short minimal-counterexample proof: delete a vertex, take the disconnected color components in the smaller Gallai coloring, and use the homogeneity of colors between components to force the same color to remain disconnected after the vertex is restored.

Baltic Way 1997 P19(b) partitions the edges of \(K_9\) into four Hamiltonian cycles. IMC 2013 Day 1 P3 has a looser but related complete-graph edge-cover viewpoint, where all pairs of students are covered by selected cliques.

The IMC trip problem covers all edges of a complete graph by structured vertex blocks rather than decomposing them exactly; Baltic Way 1997 P19(b) is a tighter edge-disjoint Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition problem.

Kolmogorov 2009 R1 is the direct n=100 olympiad instance of Bondy's theorem: the graph is Hamiltonian and has more than 100^2/4 edges, so the balanced K_{50,50} exception is impossible and all requested cycle lengths follow.
The Kolmogorov problem is best recorded as an external-theorem application of Bondy's dense Hamiltonian pancyclicity theorem, not as a local Dirac or Ore consequence.

Bondy's theorem is a pancyclicity upgrade in the same Hamiltonian-cycle family as Dirac's theorem: Dirac gives a Hamiltonian cycle from minimum degree at least n/2, while Bondy starts with a Hamiltonian cycle and the corresponding dense edge threshold to force all cycle lengths.

Dirac is the school-level Hamiltonicity tool behind many dense graph arguments; Bondy's theorem is the stronger external pancyclic analogue once Hamiltonicity and the n^2/4 edge threshold are available.

Bondy's theorem is closely tied to the Ore/Dirac Hamiltonian threshold tradition: Ore supplies Hamiltonicity from degree sums, and Bondy's pancyclic theorem is the external result that turns dense Hamiltonicity into cycles of every length up to the balanced bipartite exception.
Ore's theorem has a compact olympiad proof via maximal non-Hamiltonian completion, whereas Bondy's pancyclic conclusion requires a substantially more delicate external cycle-length argument.

Bondy and Mantel share the n^2/4 threshold and the balanced complete bipartite extremal graph. Mantel says this threshold forces a triangle unless the graph is bipartite extremal; Bondy says that with Hamiltonicity it forces every cycle length unless the same extremal graph occurs.

Mantel is the short school-level shadow of the same extremal threshold: Bondy's theorem keeps the K_{n/2,n/2} obstruction but strengthens the conclusion from a triangle to full pancyclicity under Hamiltonicity.

Bondy's exceptional graph is the r=2 Turan extremal graph. The theorem belongs to the same extremal-structure theme, but adds Hamiltonicity and obtains a cycle spectrum rather than only a forbidden-clique edge bound.
Turan's theorem explains the balanced multipartite extremal object behind the n^2/4 boundary; Bondy's theorem is a pancyclic Hamiltonian strengthening at the bipartite boundary.

Both cards are dense-graph Hamiltonian tools. The complete-graph-minus lemma gives an olympiad-size longest-path argument for a Hamiltonian path under a very strong density assumption, while Bondy is the much stronger external theorem forcing all cycle lengths at the Mantel threshold once a Hamiltonian cycle is given.

The complete-graph-minus lemma is a local school analogue of the density-plus-path-closure style; it should not be mistaken for a proof of Bondy's pancyclic theorem, whose threshold and conclusion are much sharper.

Both cards sit in the Hamiltonian-cycle part of the graph database, but with different flavors: Bondy forces cycles of all lengths from density plus one Hamiltonian cycle, while Baltic Way 1997 asks for packing edge-disjoint Hamiltonian cycles in a complete graph.

The Baltic Way problem is a constructive Hamiltonian-cycle packing task; Bondy's theorem is a dense extremal pancyclicity theorem and should be linked as thematic background rather than as a solution prerequisite.

Both cards concern forcing large specified cycles, but by opposite mechanisms: Bondy uses high density and Hamiltonicity to force every length, while the Kolmogorov 2014 problem uses low-degree local triangle structure and a heavy structural classification to obtain two 100-cycles.
Kolmogorov 2014 is a useful contrast to Bondy: it is a cycle-forcing problem, but not a dense Hamiltonian pancyclicity application.

The Gallai lemma is the structural opposite of the USA TST rainbow-triangle count: it studies complete-graph edge-colorings with no rainbow triangle, while the TST problem counts how many rainbow triangles can be forced when monochromatic triangles are forbidden. Both problems hinge on the three possible triangle color patterns in an edge-colored complete graph.

USA TST 2013 December P1 is a quantitative cousin of the Gallai setting: instead of using no-rainbow-triangle structure to force a disconnected color class, it counts local repeated-color triangles in a complete graph edge-coloring and maximizes the complementary rainbow triangles.

Gallai's lemma forbids all rainbow triangles and extracts global information about color-class connectivity. The small-k half of IMO 1998 C6 goes in the other direction: for k=3 every triangle would need to be rainbow, and for k=4 the proof again treats colors on complete-graph triangles as the main obstruction.

IMO 1998 C6 is not a Gallai-coloring application, but it is a close rainbow-triangle relative: both arguments turn an edge-coloring of a complete graph into constraints on the possible color patterns of its triangles.

The Gallai lemma is a no-rainbow-triangle theorem for complete-graph edge-colorings, whereas Simon Marais 2020 B4 constructs a large rainbow clique in a distance-coloring of a complete graph. The shared motif is the translation from geometric data to colors on complete-graph edges and then to rainbow subgraphs.

Simon Marais 2020 B4 is a constructive rainbow-clique problem rather than a connected-color-class theorem. It is still a useful distant neighbor because its graph reformulation asks for rainbow structure inside a complete graph whose edge colors come from geometry.

Gallai's lemma and Schweitzer 2012 P3 both use connected monochromatic components as the bridge from an edge-coloring to a global obstruction. Gallai says that in a three-color complete graph with no rainbow triangle, not all three spanning color classes can be connected; Schweitzer 2012 P3 converts small two-color components into a forbidden low vertex-coloring.

Schweitzer 2012 P3 is a chromatic-number version of the same component philosophy: instead of using no-rainbow triangles, it builds an auxiliary bipartite multigraph from red and blue components and turns its edge-coloring into a vertex coloring of the original graph.

The Gallai lemma concludes that some color class is disconnected; Schweitzer 2011 P2 uses the complementary cut idea in a two-color dense graph, where a disconnected red class forces all cut edges to be blue and then degree counting gives a large blue connected subgraph.

Schweitzer 2011 P2 is a dense-graph and two-color analogue of the disconnected-color-class move. It does not involve rainbow triangles, but it uses the same basic structural fact that once one color fails to connect across a cut, the other color controls the cut.

The Gallai card is a small structural theorem about complete-graph edge-colorings and rainbow triangles. Schweitzer 2009 P1 is a more distant extremal-coloring relative: its cards are complete-graph edge-colorings designed to make selected K15 subgraphs rainbow.

Schweitzer 2009 P1 shares the complete-graph edge-coloring and rainbow-subgraph language, but it is a covering/counting construction rather than a no-rainbow structural lemma. The relation is useful mainly as a broader rainbow-clique motif link.

Miklos-Schweitzer 2016 P2 reduces non-collinearity to a three-color complete-graph coloring with no rainbow triangle and all three color classes connected, contradicting the Gallai disconnected-color lemma.
The problem uses only the three-color disconnected-color lemma for Gallai colorings, not the full Gallai partition theorem.

IMC 1997 P6(b) and IMC 2003 Day 2 P4 both use uniform hypergraph language: finite edges of equal size are central. The mechanisms differ strongly, since P6(b) proves a finite transversal theorem by trace induction, while the Steiner-triple problem algebraizes a 3-uniform design.

The Steiner-triple card is another uniform-hypergraph problem in the IMC set. Unlike the transversal theorem for intersecting families, it relies on unique pair completion and an \(\mathbb F_2\)-group structure rather than on cross-intersecting induction.

In hypergraph terms, IMC 1997 P6(b) studies a uniform family with matching number one and proves a finite transversal for pairwise intersections. IMC 2011 Day 2 P2 is nearby in the matching/transversal vocabulary, but aims for a perfect matching of 3-partite triples under density assumptions.

The married-triples problem is related by the hypergraph matching viewpoint: it seeks a spanning matching of allowed triples, whereas IMC 1997 P6(b) starts from an intersecting uniform hypergraph and builds a finite set hitting all pairwise intersections.
